claim: Absence seizures are characterized by brief periods of unconsciousness accompanied by lapses in motor function that can occur hundreds of times throughout the day.
source: Absence seizures are characterized by brief periods of unconsciousness accompanied by lapses in motor function that can occur hundreds of times throughout the day.
evidence: This is a well-established clinical characterization of absence seizures, drawing from established scientific consensus.

claim: Approximately a third of people living with absence epilepsy experience treatment-resistant attention impairments outside of seizure periods.
source: Outside of these frequent moments of unconsciousness, approximately a third of people living with the disorder experience treatment-resistant attention impairments.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge about the clinical presentation of absence epilepsy.

claim: Convergent evidence suggests prefrontal cortex (PFC) dysfunction may underlie attention impairments in absence epilepsy patients.
source: Convergent evidence suggests prefrontal cortex (PFC) dysfunction may underlie attention impairments in affected patients.
evidence: This is based on inference from multiple lines of evidence mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: Scn8a+/- mice exhibit altered parvalbumin interneuron (PVIN) output in the medial PFC (mPFC) in vitro.
source: In Scn8a+/-mice, we find altered parvalbumin interneuron (PVIN) output in the medial PFC (mPFC) in vitro and PVIN hypoactivity along with reductions in gamma power during cue presentation in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from slice physiology experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Scn8a+/- mice exhibit PVIN hypoactivity during cue presentation in vivo.
source: In Scn8a+/-mice, we find altered parvalbumin interneuron (PVIN) output in the medial PFC (mPFC) in vitro and PVIN hypoactivity along with reductions in gamma power during cue presentation in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry data collected during behavioral testing.

claim: Scn8a+/- mice exhibit reductions in gamma power during cue presentation in vivo.
source: In Scn8a+/-mice, we find altered parvalbumin interneuron (PVIN) output in the medial PFC (mPFC) in vitro and PVIN hypoactivity along with reductions in gamma power during cue presentation in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by ECoG recordings during behavioral testing.

claim: Scn8a+/- mice show poorer attention performance that is associated with PVIN hypoactivity and reduced gamma power.
source: This was associated with poorer attention performance in Scn8a+/-mice that could be rescued by gamma-frequency optogenetic stimulation of PVINs.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the attentional engagement task combined with electrophysiological measurements.

claim: Gamma-frequency optogenetic stimulation of PVINs can rescue attention performance deficits in Scn8a+/- mice.
source: This was associated with poorer attention performance in Scn8a+/-mice that could be rescued by gamma-frequency optogenetic stimulation of PVINs.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic manipulation experiments during behavioral testing.

claim: Cue-related PVIN activity is an important mechanism for attention.
source: This highlights cue-related PVIN activity as an important mechanism for attention and suggests PVINs may represent a therapeutic target for cognitive comorbidities in absence epilepsy.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing correlation between PVIN activity and attention performance.

claim: PVINs may represent a therapeutic target for cognitive comorbidities in absence epilepsy.
source: This highlights cue-related PVIN activity as an important mechanism for attention and suggests PVINs may represent a therapeutic target for cognitive comorbidities in absence epilepsy.
evidence: This is speculative, based on the experimental findings that optogenetic stimulation of PVINs can rescue attention deficits.

claim: Attention deficits in absence epilepsy do not respond to current treatments.
source: One such example is absence epilepsy, where attention deficits do not respond to current treatments and are a significant predictor of adverse long-term outcome across patients (Masur et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous clinical research.

claim: Attention deficits are a significant predictor of adverse long-term outcome in absence epilepsy patients.
source: One such example is absence epilepsy, where attention deficits do not respond to current treatments and are a significant predictor of adverse long-term outcome across patients (Masur et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous clinical research.

claim: Absence seizures are diagnosed by a distinct EEG pattern: bilateral synchronous 3–4 Hz spike-and-wave discharge (SWD).
source: Absence seizures are diagnosed by a distinct EEG pattern: bilateral synchronous 3–4 Hz spike-and-wave discharge (SWD), which manifests as brief periods of unconsciousness accompanied by a lapse in motor function (Gibbs et al., 1935; Panayiotopoulos, 1999).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge supported by historical citations.

claim: Typical absence seizures are present in 10–15% of all epilepsy syndromes.
source: Typical absence seizures are present in 10–15% of all epilepsy syndromes, and can occur hundreds of times throughout the day (Berg et al., 1999; Panayiotopoulos, 2001; Posner, 2008).
evidence: This is epidemiological data supported by citations.

claim: Animal models reliably capture many aspects of the absence seizure phenotype.
source: While animal models reliably capture many aspects of the absence seizure phenotype (Coenen and Van Luijtelaar, 1987; Meeren et al., 2005; Papale et al., 2009; Vergnes et al., 1982), there has been little direct exploration of attention performance in rodent models of absence epilepsy or of the underlying mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous animal model studies.

claim: There has been little direct exploration of attention performance in rodent models of absence epilepsy.
source: While animal models reliably capture many aspects of the absence seizure phenotype (Coenen and Van Luijtelaar, 1987; Meeren et al., 2005; Papale et al., 2009; Vergnes et al., 1982), there has been little direct exploration of attention performance in rodent models of absence epilepsy or of the underlying mechanisms.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, supported by the absence of citations for such studies.

claim: The dorsolateral PFC supports many components of attention in humans and primates.
source: Several studies point to the dorsolateral PFC supporting many of these components in humans and primates (Barceló et al., 2000; Gregoriou et al., 2014; Rossi et al., 2007; Zanto et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The prelimbic medial PFC (mPFC) is the closest functional homolog of human dorsolateral PFC in rodents.
source: This is strengthened by lesion data from rodents of the closest functional homolog of human dorsolateral PFC, the prelimbic medial PFC (mPFC) (Chudasama and Muir, 2001; Kahn et al., 2012; Muir et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by citations to lesion studies.

claim: Medial PFC PVINs show attention-related activity.
source: Recent advances have allowed for more exploration into cell-type-specific mechanisms of attention, revealing that fast-spiking GABAergic interneurons, or parvalbumin-expressing interneurons (PVINs), show attention-related activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: Medial PFC PVINs represent rule information in a flexible attentional shifting task.
source: Medial PFC PVINs have been shown to represent rule information in a flexible attentional shifting task (Rikhye et al., 2018), while population increases in PVIN activity during the delay period prior to cue onset are associated with correct choices in a sustained attention task (Kim et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Population increases in PVIN activity during the delay period prior to cue onset are associated with correct choices in a sustained attention task.
source: Medial PFC PVINs have been shown to represent rule information in a flexible attentional shifting task (Rikhye et al., 2018), while population increases in PVIN activity during the delay period prior to cue onset are associated with correct choices in a sustained attention task (Kim et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Scn8a+/- mice performed significantly worse than WT mice at intermediate cue lengths (2 s and 1 s) in the AET.
source: However, Scn8a+/-mice performed significantly worse than WT mice at intermediate cue lengths (2 s and 1 s), suggesting an impairment in attentional engagement (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: When cue length was kept constant within trial blocks, there were no differences in accuracy between Scn8a+/- and WT groups.
source: Importantly, when we kept the cue length constant within trial blocks, presumably reducing attentional load, there were no differences in accuracy between groups (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There were no differences in omissions between Scn8a+/- and WT groups.
source: We also quantified omissions, trials in which the animal took longer than 5 s following cue termination to make a choice (likely because the animals failed to perceive the presence of the cue) and found no differences between groups (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The lack of difference in performance during single cue-length blocks or omissions suggests that observed differences on the AET are specific to increases in attentional load rather than an effect of reduced Scn8a on visual perception or discrimination.
source: This lack of difference in performance during single cue-length blocks or omissions suggests that observed differences on the AET are specific to increases in attentional load rather than an effect of reduced Scn8a on visual perception or discrimination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of behavioral results.

claim: There was no effect of group on reaction time in the AET.
source: There was no effect of group on reaction time (seconds between cue termination and port selection); however, all mice had increased reaction time for incorrect trials, which has been correlated with impaired attention in other paradigms (Fitzpatrick et al., 2017; Weissberg et al., 1990; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: All mice had increased reaction time for incorrect trials.
source: There was no effect of group on reaction time (seconds between cue termination and port selection); however, all mice had increased reaction time for incorrect trials, which has been correlated with impaired attention in other paradigms (Fitzpatrick et al., 2017; Weissberg et al., 1990; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Increased reaction time for incorrect trials has been correlated with impaired attention in other paradigms.
source: There was no effect of group on reaction time (seconds between cue termination and port selection); however, all mice had increased reaction time for incorrect trials, which has been correlated with impaired attention in other paradigms (Fitzpatrick et al., 2017; Weissberg et al., 1990; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Scn8a+/- mice had a higher repetitive responding score in comparison to WT littermates.
source: We observed that Scn8a+/-mice had a higher repetitive responding in comparison to WT littermates (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: There were no significant differences between Scn8a+/- and WT groups in the three-chamber sociability task.
source: Finally, to examine whether Scn8a+/-mice might exhibit broad behavioral impairments, we assayed sociability utilizing the three-chamber task and the hippocampal-dependent object recognition task and observed no significant differences between groups (Figure 1G–L).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figures 1G-L.

claim: There were no significant differences between Scn8a+/- and WT groups in the object recognition task.
source: Finally, to examine whether Scn8a+/-mice might exhibit broad behavioral impairments, we assayed sociability utilizing the three-chamber task and the hippocampal-dependent object recognition task and observed no significant differences between groups (Figure 1G–L).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figures 1G-L.

claim: Absence epilepsy patients experience attention impairments during interictal periods and even when seizures are well controlled with anti-epileptic drugs.
source: Absence epilepsy patients experience attention impairments during interictal periods and even when seizures are well controlled with anti-epileptic drugs (Barone et al., 2020), suggesting that attention dysfunction is not purely due to the periodic losses of consciousness associated with SWDs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical research.

claim: Attention dysfunction in absence epilepsy is not purely due to the periodic losses of consciousness associated with SWDs.
source: Absence epilepsy patients experience attention impairments during interictal periods and even when seizures are well controlled with anti-epileptic drugs (Barone et al., 2020), suggesting that attention dysfunction is not purely due to the periodic losses of consciousness associated with SWDs.
evidence: This is an inference based on clinical observations cited in the manuscript.

claim: Absence seizure prevalence is highest in periods of quiet waking.
source: Additionally, absence seizure prevalence is highest in periods of quiet waking (Barone et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Engaging in the task reduced seizure frequency in Scn8a+/- mice in comparison to that recorded in their home cage.
source: Engaging in the task reduced seizure frequency in Scn8a+/-mice in comparison to that recorded in their home cage (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by ECoG data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There was no difference in the Ø (7–10 Hz) or β (10–20 Hz) range ECoG spectral power between correct trials and incorrect trials in Scn8a+/- mice.
source: We found no difference in the Ø (7–10 Hz) or β (10–20 Hz) range (Figure 2F and G) which encompass the fundamental and 2nd harmonic frequency bands for absence seizures, respectively (Sorokin et al., 2017; Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by ECoG data shown in Figures 2F and G.

claim: The Ø (7–10 Hz) and β (10–20 Hz) frequency ranges encompass the fundamental and 2nd harmonic frequency bands for absence seizures, respectively.
source: We found no difference in the Ø (7–10 Hz) or β (10–20 Hz) range (Figure 2F and G) which encompass the fundamental and 2nd harmonic frequency bands for absence seizures, respectively (Sorokin et al., 2017; Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In Scn8a+/- mice, there were no differences in power across cue lengths in seizure-related frequency bands.
source: In Scn8a+/-mice, there were no differences in power across cue lengths (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: This is supported by ECoG data shown in Figures 2I-K.

claim: The lack of difference in seizure band power during correct versus incorrect trials suggests that seizures do not contribute to AET errors in Scn8a+/- mice.
source: As we would expect a spectral power increase with any seizure activity (example SWD, Figure 2H), the lack of difference in seizure band power during correct versus incorrect trials suggests that seizures do not contribute to AET errors in Scn8a+/-mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ECoG data analysis.

claim: On average, in Scn8a+/- mice, ~1% of trials had seizures within 10 s of the trial.
source: On average, in Scn8a+/-mice, ~1% of trials had seizures within 10 s of the trial, and in fewer than 1% of trials (0.24%) were we able to detect seizures during the cue (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Table 1.

claim: In fewer than 1% of trials (0.24%) in Scn8a+/- mice were seizures detected during the cue.
source: On average, in Scn8a+/-mice, ~1% of trials had seizures within 10 s of the trial, and in fewer than 1% of trials (0.24%) were we able to detect seizures during the cue (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Table 1.

claim: Power in seizure-related frequency bands was not different between Scn8a+/- mice and WTs for the intermediate cue.
source: Finally, power in seizure-related frequency bands was not different between Scn8a+/-mice and WTs for the intermediate cue (Figure 2L), where the relative difference in performance was greatest.
evidence: This is supported by ECoG data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: SWDs are largely absent while animals perform the AET.
source: This indicates that SWDs are largely absent while animals perform the AET, and differences in absence seizure activity do not explain reductions in performance in Scn8a+/-mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the seizure frequency data during task performance.

claim: Differences in absence seizure activity do not explain reductions in performance in Scn8a+/- mice.
source: This indicates that SWDs are largely absent while animals perform the AET, and differences in absence seizure activity do not explain reductions in performance in Scn8a+/-mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correlation between seizure activity and performance.

claim: Photoinhibition of mPFC during cue presentation reduces accuracy in the AET.
source: In the AET, we silenced mPFC during the variable cue period (Figure 3C) where we hypothesized attention is most heavily engaged, and observed a small reduction in performance with continuous light stimulation (Figure 3D) without a significant change in reaction time.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic manipulation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Photoinhibition of mPFC during the fixed cue period in the VDST does not affect performance or reaction time.
source: When we photo-inhibited mPFC during the fixed cue period in the VDST (Figure 3E), there were no differences in the percentage of correct choices or reaction time (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic manipulation data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Photoinhibition of mPFC during the variable delay period in the VDST reduces performance.
source: However, when we silenced mPFC activity during the variable delay period (Figure 3G), light stimulation reduced performance (Figure 3H), without a significant difference in reaction time.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic manipulation data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The AET is linked to the mPFC.
source: This suggests that the AET is linked to the mPFC, and that mPFC activation plays a role during cue presentation in an attention-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the optogenetic manipulation results.

claim: mPFC activation plays a role during cue presentation in an attention-dependent manner.
source: This suggests that the AET is linked to the mPFC, and that mPFC activation plays a role during cue presentation in an attention-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of mPFC inhibition in the AET versus VDST.

claim: Scn8a+/- mice exhibit a significant reduction in a late source present over Layer 2/3 in mPFC slice recordings.
source: We used a pharmacological approach to identify these distinct CSD components (Figure 4D–H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and found a significant reduction specifically in one feature – a late source present over Layer 2/3 (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by slice electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The late source over Layer 2/3 represents a disynaptic response given its sensitivity to post-synaptic blockers, DNQX and CPP.
source: Pharmacological characterization indicated that this source represents a disynaptic response given its sensitivity to post-synaptic blockers, DNQX and CPP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological manipulation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Scn8a+/- mice may have attenuated recruitment of local mPFC GABAergic interneurons.
source: Thus, we hypothesized that Scn8a+/-mice may have attenuated recruitment of local mPFC GABAergic interneurons.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the interpretation of the CSD data.

claim: The percentage of synaptic failures within the 40 Hz train was significantly increased in Scn8a+/- mice compared to WT.
source: We recorded significantly more failures in Scn8a+/-mice in comparison to WT (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The spike reduction rate with 40 Hz PVIN activation was retained in Scn8a+/- mice.
source: We observed that the spike reduction rate with 40 Hz PVIN activation was retained in Scn8a+/-mice (Figure 5E), indicating that PVINs are still capable of inhibiting pyramidal neuron output when stimulated optogenetically.
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: PVINs are still capable of inhibiting pyramidal neuron output when stimulated optogenetically in Scn8a+/- mice.
source: We observed that the spike reduction rate with 40 Hz PVIN activation was retained in Scn8a+/-mice (Figure 5E), indicating that PVINs are still capable of inhibiting pyramidal neuron output when stimulated optogenetically.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spike reduction data.

claim: For correct trials, PVIN activity was consistently modulated only at intermediate cue lengths for both WT and Scn8a+/- groups.
source: We found that for correct trials PVIN activity was consistently modulated only at intermediate cue lengths for both groups (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: For incorrect trials, there was no significant modulation in PVIN GCaMP signals at any cue length.
source: However, for incorrect trials, we found no significant modulation in PVIN GCaMP signals at any cue length.
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry data analysis.

claim: Average PVIN activity was reduced during the intermediate cue for Scn8a+/- mice compared to WT.
source: When we compared cue activity between WT and Scn8a+/-mice, only for the intermediate cue was average dF/F decreased in Scn8a+/-mice (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Peak amplitude of PVIN activity was significantly reduced in Scn8a+/- mice at long and intermediate cues, but not the short cue.
source: The peak amplitude was also significantly reduced in Scn8a+/-mice at long and intermediate cues, but not the short cue (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Time to peak PVIN activity was not different between WT and Scn8a+/- groups.
source: Time to peak PVIN activity was not different between groups (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Features of cue-related PVIN activity patterns are linked to the accuracy of the upcoming choice.
source: Across (Figure 6G) and within (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) cue lengths for both groups the models could identify accurate trials, as determined by receiver operating characteristic area under the curve scores (ROC-AUC, Fawcett, 2006). This suggests that broadly, features of cue-related PVIN activity patterns are linked to the accuracy of the upcoming choice.
evidence: This is supported by machine learning classification analysis of fiber photometry data.

claim: 40 Hz optogenetic activation of PVINs increased the percentage of correct choices for Scn8a+/- mice specifically at the intermediate cue.
source: Activation of PVINs at gamma frequency (40 Hz) increased the percentage of correct choices for PV-Cre;Scn8a+/- mice specifically at the intermediate cue (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic manipulation data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 40 Hz stimulation was capable of increasing ECoG power in the 30–50 Hz range in Scn8a+/- mice expressing ChR2 in PVINs.
source: We also observed that 40 Hz stimulation was capable of increasing ECoG power in the 30–50 Hz range in a separate cohort of mice Scn8a+/- mice expressing ChR2 in PVINs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ECoG data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effect of 40 Hz stimulation on performance was not observed in Scn8a+/- mice that underwent the same experimental protocol with a control eYFP virus.
source: Importantly, this effect was not observed in PV-Cre;Scn8a+/- mice that underwent the same experimental protocol with a control eYFP virus (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is a control experiment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: VPA significantly reduced seizure burden in Scn8a+/- mice.
source: WT and Scn8a+/-mice were treated twice daily with saline or the anti-epileptic drug, Valproic Acid (VPA), the latter of which significantly reduced seizure burden in Scn8a+/-mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by ECoG data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D.

claim: There was no effect of VPA on accuracy in either WT or Scn8a+/- groups.
source: Although Scn8a+/-mice exhibited reduced performance compared to WTs, there was no effect of VPA on accuracy in either group (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Scn8a+/- mice have reduced ECoG spectral power for both the long and intermediate cue during the AET.
source: AET performance was reduced in Scn8a+/-mice (Figure 8C) with concomitant reductions in spectral power for both the long and intermediate cue (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: This is supported by ECoG data shown in Figures 8D and E.

claim: For the intermediate cue, there was a significant reduction in high gamma activity (60–90 Hz) in Scn8a+/- mice.
source: Specifically for the intermediate cue, there was a significant reduction in high gamma activity (60–90 Hz) in Scn8a+/-mice.
evidence: This is supported by ECoG data analysis.

claim: For the short cue, there were no differences in power across any frequency band between WT and Scn8a+/- mice.
source: For the short cue we observed no differences in power across any frequency band (Figure 8F), which is consistent with the absence of behavioral differences or evoked PVIN activity at this cue length.
evidence: This is supported by ECoG data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The absence of power differences at the short cue is consistent with the absence of behavioral differences or evoked PVIN activity at this cue length.
source: For the short cue we observed no differences in power across any frequency band (Figure 8F), which is consistent with the absence of behavioral differences or evoked PVIN activity at this cue length.
evidence: This is an inference connecting multiple experimental observations.

claim: Increases in cue-related mPFC PVIN activity are associated with correct choices during the AET.
source: Our findings demonstrate that increases in cue-related mPFC PVIN activity are associated with correct choices during a novel attentional engagement task (AET).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the fiber photometry data.

claim: PVIN activity is reduced in Scn8a+/- mice along with poorer performance on the AET.
source: Additionally, PVIN activity is reduced in Scn8a+/-mice along with poorer performance on the AET.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the fiber photometry and behavioral data.

claim: This study provides the first evidence of both the behavioral manifestation and a circuit biomarker of attention impairments in an animal model of absence epilepsy.
source: These results also provide the first evidence of both the behavioral manifestation and a circuit biomarker of attention impairments in an animal model of absence epilepsy, one of the most commonly presenting cognitive comorbidities associated with the syndrome.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: The recruitment of PVINs and gamma activity represent key circuit mechanisms during attentional engagement.
source: Further, our results suggest that the recruitment of PVINs and gamma activity represent key circuit mechanisms during attentional engagement.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined experimental findings.

claim: Attention impairments are present even in interictal periods in absence epilepsy patients.
source: These attention impairments are present even in interictal periods (Conant et al., 2010; D'Agati et al., 2012; Vega et al., 2010) and do not respond to current anti-epileptic drugs (Glauser et al., 2010; Masur et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical research.

claim: Attention impairments in absence epilepsy do not respond to current anti-epileptic drugs.
source: These attention impairments are present even in interictal periods (Conant et al., 2010; D'Agati et al., 2012; Vega et al., 2010) and do not respond to current anti-epileptic drugs (Glauser et al., 2010; Masur et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical research.

claim: Mutations in Scn8a have been observed in patients with absence epilepsy, intellectual disability, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, and autism spectrum disorders.
source: Mutations in Scn8a have been observed in patients with absence epilepsy, intellectual disability, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, and autism spectrum disorders (Liu et al., 2019; Papale et al., 2009; Trudeau et al., 2006; Wagnon et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical and genetic studies.

claim: Scn8a encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel, NaV1.6.
source: Scn8a encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel, NaV1.6, and mice with reduced NaV1.6 expression have frequent and well-characterized absence seizures, due at least in part to specific hypofunction of inhibitory neurons in the thalamus (Makinson et al., 2017; Papale et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the gene product.

claim: Mice with reduced NaV1.6 expression have frequent and well-characterized absence seizures, due at least in part to specific hypofunction of inhibitory neurons in the thalamus.
source: Scn8a encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel, NaV1.6, and mice with reduced NaV1.6 expression have frequent and well-characterized absence seizures, due at least in part to specific hypofunction of inhibitory neurons in the thalamus (Makinson et al., 2017; Papale et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: On average, mice learned the AET association in 6 training sessions.
source: On average, mice learned this association in 6 training sessions, and there were no group differences in how long it took mice to reach stable performance or criterion (3 days at greater than 70% correct or 2 days greater than 90% correct, Figure 1A, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral training data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There were no group differences in how long it took mice to reach stable performance or criterion in the AET.
source: On average, mice learned this association in 6 training sessions, and there were no group differences in how long it took mice to reach stable performance or criterion (3 days at greater than 70% correct or 2 days greater than 90% correct, Figure 1A, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral training data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Optogenetic activation of interneurons has been shown to inactivate cortical network activity.
source: As optogenetic activation of interneurons has been shown to inactivate cortical network activity (Guo et al., 2014), this would allow for mPFC inhibition during distinct task epochs (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Blue light can inhibit neuronal activity continuously throughout the durations used in the AET.
source: First, we confirmed in vitro that blue light could inhibit neuronal activity continuously throughout the durations used in the AET (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by slice electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Continuous blue light can hyperpolarize neurons at pulse lengths of 5 s, 2 s, and 0.5 s.
source: Similarly, we observed that continuous blue light can hyperpolarize neurons at the same pulse lengths (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by slice electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Photoinhibition with blue light reduces performance in the AET without affecting reaction time.
source: Photoinhibition with blue light reduces performance (left, two-way RM ANOVA, group effect F(1,18) = 6.990, p=0.0165, n=6), without affecting reaction time (right, two-way RM ANOVA, F(1,18) = 3.323, p=0.0850, n=6) in the AET.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic manipulation data with statistical analysis.

claim: Stimulation during the delay reduces performance in the VDST without altering reaction time.
source: Stimulation during the delay reduces performance in the VDST (left, paired t test, p=0.0140) without altering reaction time (right, paired t test, p=0.1268).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic manipulation data with statistical analysis.

claim: PVINs have been classically linked to feedforward inhibition, a type of disynaptic inhibition important for gating cortical responses.
source: PVINs have been classically linked to feedforward inhibition, a type of disynaptic inhibition important for gating cortical responses (Delevich et al., 2015; Swadlow, 2003), as well as successful attentional performance and cognitively associated gamma oscillations (Cardin et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2016a; Sohal et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PVINs are linked to successful attentional performance and cognitively associated gamma oscillations.
source: PVINs have been classically linked to feedforward inhibition, a type of disynaptic inhibition important for gating cortical responses (Delevich et al., 2015; Swadlow, 2003), as well as successful attentional performance and cognitively associated gamma oscillations (Cardin et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2016a; Sohal et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Individuals with absence epilepsy exhibit reduced functional activation of the PFC that correlates with attentional impairments.
source: Additionally, individuals with absence epilepsy exhibit reduced functional activation of the PFC that correlates with attentional impairments (Killory et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical neuroimaging research.

claim: In patients, SWD is prominent over the frontal cortex, suggesting frontal dysfunction.
